# Thermochemistry — 2.3 Enthalpy

::: concept T-enthalpy
term: Enthalpy
definition: [p.11: "Enthalpy (H) is a property of a system equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume:"]
plain: Enthalpy is a property of a system: its internal energy plus its pressure times its volume. [p.11: "equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume"]
why: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on where the system starts and ends, not on the path. [p.11: "enthalpy is a state function: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states of the system."]
misconception: Wrong: like heat, enthalpy depends on the path taken. | Right: enthalpy is a state function; ΔH depends only on the initial and final states. [p.11: "Unlike heat, which depends on the path taken, enthalpy is a state function"]
:::

::: formula EQ-2.2
name: Definition of enthalpy
latex: H = U + PV
where: H = enthalpy; U = internal energy; P = pressure; V = volume. [p.11: "Enthalpy (H) is a property of a system equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume"]
holds-when: This is how the book defines enthalpy. [p.11: "Enthalpy (H) is a property of a system equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume"]
source: [p.11: "Enthalpy (H) is a property of a system equal to its internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume:"]
check: H = U + P * V
rearrange: U = H - P * V
:::

::: concept T-enthalpy-change
term: Enthalpy change
definition: [p.11: "The enthalpy change (ΔH) for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system:"]
plain: At constant pressure, the enthalpy change is the heat the system takes in or gives out. [p.11: "The enthalpy change (ΔH) for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system"]
why: Chemists rarely measure enthalpy itself; they measure changes in enthalpy. [p.11: "Chemists rarely measure enthalpy itself; instead they measure changes in enthalpy."]
example: Burning methane releases 890 kJ per mole, so its ΔH is −890 kJ. [p.11: "the combustion of methane releases 890 kJ of heat per mole of methane burned, so ΔH = −890 kJ."]
misconception: Wrong: a negative ΔH means the system absorbed heat. | Right: an exothermic reaction releases heat, so its ΔH is negative. [p.11: "For an exothermic reaction, the system releases heat, so ΔH is negative."]
:::

::: formula EQ-2.3
name: Enthalpy change equals heat at constant pressure
latex: \Delta H = q_p
where: ΔH = enthalpy change; q_p = heat absorbed or released by the system at constant pressure. [p.11: "The enthalpy change (ΔH) for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system"]
holds-when: Only for a process carried out at constant pressure. [p.11: "for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system"]
source: [p.11: "The enthalpy change (ΔH) for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system:"]
example: ΔH is positive for an endothermic reaction and negative for an exothermic one. [p.11: "For an endothermic reaction, the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive. For an exothermic reaction, the system releases heat, so ΔH is negative."]
:::

::: worked-example WE-2.2
title: Classifying a Reaction
source: Example 2.2 [p.11: "The reaction N_2(g) + O_2(g) → 2 NO(g) has ΔH = +180.5 kJ."]
problem: Is N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO(g), with ΔH = +180.5 kJ, endothermic or exothermic? [p.11: "The reaction N_2(g) + O_2(g) → 2 NO(g) has ΔH = +180.5 kJ. Is it endothermic or exothermic?"]
step: Look at the sign of ΔH: +180.5 kJ is positive.
step: A positive ΔH means the system absorbs heat, so the reaction is endothermic.
result: The reaction is endothermic because ΔH is positive. [p.11: "ΔH is positive, so the reaction absorbs heat and is endothermic."]
:::

::: question Q-2.3-01
type: mcq
bloom: understand
ask: The combustion of methane has ΔH = −890 kJ. What does the negative sign tell you?
option A: The reaction releases heat, so it is exothermic.
option B: The reaction absorbs heat, so it is endothermic.
option C: The reaction involves no heat at all.
option D: The pressure must have changed during the reaction.
answer: A
why: A negative ΔH means the system releases heat, as in an exothermic reaction. [p.11: "For an exothermic reaction, the system releases heat, so ΔH is negative."]
why-not B: Endothermic reactions have a positive ΔH. [p.11: "For an endothermic reaction, the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive."]
why-not C: At constant pressure, ΔH is the heat absorbed or released. [p.11: "equals the heat absorbed or released by the system"]
why-not D: The book links ΔH to heat at constant pressure, not to a change in pressure. [p.11: "for a process carried out at constant pressure"]
covers: LO-2.3-2, T-enthalpy-change, T-exothermic-process
:::

::: question Q-2.3-02
type: numeric
bloom: apply
ask: A process at constant pressure absorbs 12.0 kJ of heat. What is ΔH for the process?
calc: dH = 12.0[kJ] => 12.0[kJ]
answer: 12.0[kJ]
why: At constant pressure ΔH equals the heat absorbed, and absorbing heat makes ΔH positive. [p.11: "The enthalpy change (ΔH) for a process carried out at constant pressure equals the heat absorbed or released by the system"] [p.11: "the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive"]
covers: LO-2.3-1, EQ-2.3
:::

::: question Q-2.3-03
type: cloze
bloom: remember
ask: Enthalpy is a ____ function: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states of the system.
answer: state
why: The book calls enthalpy a state function. [p.11: "enthalpy is a state function: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states of the system."]
covers: LO-2.3-1, T-enthalpy
:::

::: question Q-2.3-04
type: tf
bloom: understand
ask: For an endothermic reaction, ΔH is negative.
answer: false
why: For an endothermic reaction the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive. [p.11: "For an endothermic reaction, the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive."]
covers: LO-2.3-2, T-endothermic-process
:::
